tagline: Follow the Snake River canyon where springs emerge from rock
intro: US 30 drops into the Hagerman Valley and a canyon of the Snake River, where springs emerge from the east wall. Many are visible from the road, with the river in front. Visit Idaho presents Thousand Springs as one of the state’s scenic byways for its geological features, canyon views and waterfalls. Its itinerary covers 65.4 miles, with a listed driving time of one hour and 32 minutes.

US 30 was established in 1926 as part of the United States Numbered Highway System. Across southern Idaho it followed Route 2 from the Oregon line to Burley. Construction of the parallel freeway, then called I-80N and now I-84, began in the 1960s. Sections of US 30 shifted onto the freeway as it opened, but at Bliss the numbered route leaves the interstate for the byway. An earlier crossing survives south of Hagerman: Owsley Bridge, built in 1920–21, carried a former alignment of US 30 across the Snake.

From Bliss, travel southeast through Hagerman, Buhl and Filer to Twin Falls. The springs along the canyon are outlets of the Snake River Aquifer, which moves through porous volcanic rock. Beyond Twin Falls, the tourism itinerary continues to Idaho 50 and turns north to I-84, with US 93 providing another northbound connection.
notice: Springs emerge from the canyon’s east wall, with many visible beyond the river from the road.

moments.title: Thousand Springs State Park
moments.text: Thousand Springs State Park joins several landscapes under one name. It was created in 2005 by merging four existing state parks in the Hagerman Valley, with another unit added later. At Malad Gorge, the Malad River has cut a canyon 250 feet deep below a 60-foot waterfall. Elsewhere in the park, Box Canyon has walls 250 feet high and a 20-foot waterfall. The Nature Conservancy bought the Box Canyon property in 1999 and completed its transfer to the state in 2016. Ritter Island, another unit, lies between two large springs along the Snake River.

moments.title: Hagerman Fossil Beds National Monument
moments.text: Hagerman’s fossil record includes horses, camels and river otters. The deposits preserve a Pliocene landscape, with fossils dating from 3.07 million to at least four million years ago. The Hagerman Horse Quarry has yielded 20 complete skeletons as well as partial skeletons of Equus simplicidens. The beds became a National Natural Landmark in 1975 and a national monument in 1988. In 2016, researchers began a project to date individual fossil sites more closely and reconstruct the ancient landscapes they represent. The assemblage also includes birds, fish, amphibians and turtles, extending the record beyond large mammals.

moments.title: Buhl
moments.text: Buhl’s name points to the financing behind the Magic Valley’s irrigation. Founded in 1906, the town was named for Frank H. Buhl, a Pennsylvania investor in the Twin Falls South Side Project. That project introduced large-scale irrigation to the valley in the early twentieth century. US 30 passes through town, and numerous trout hatcheries operate in the surrounding area.
